hints.S37_A1: The dentist uses a SMALL MIRROR to hunt for SIGNS OF DECAY at the back of the mouth. Ask: which verb means to look at something closely and thoroughly? 'Cover' and 'block' would hide it; 'ignore' would skip it.
hints.S37_A2: The examples give it away: TOFFEE and GUM stick and pull as you bite. Ask: which adjective describes food that needs long, sticky chewing? 'Sweet' is about taste, and 'soft' food would harm no filling.
hints.S37_A3: The gel goes onto MAYA'S GUM, in exactly the right spot, before the INJECTION. Ask: which verb means to put a substance carefully onto a surface? 'Poured' suits liquid, 'polished' suits shoes, 'swallowed' sends it down.
hints.S37_A4: The drill is BEHIND THE CLOSED DOOR, and the waiting room is QUIET. Ask: does the sound reach you clearly, not at all, or dulled by that barrier? 'Inaudible' would mean nobody hears a thing.
hints.S37_A5: The purpose is stated: CATCH PROBLEMS BEFORE THEY BECOME SERIOUS, and the visits are REGULAR. Ask: which adjective describes action taken to stop trouble before it starts? 'Urgent' care comes after trouble arrives.
hints.S37_B1: EVERY SIX MONTHS signals a habit, so the verb stays present. Now count the subject: MY PARENTS AND I - more than one person. Ask: does a plural subject take the plain verb, or the one ending in -s?
hints.S37_B2: BEFORE SHE REALISED is finished past time, so the verb must be past too. Ask: is this verb regular or irregular? A regular verb simply takes -ed - and an -ing form cannot stand alone here.
hints.S37_B3: THAN sets two choices against each other: going NOW versus WAITING until the toothache gets worse. Ask: for exactly two, comparative or superlative? Short adjectives take an ending, not a helper word in front.
hints.S37_B4: Kai is measured against all of them: CHILDREN, plural, in one FAMILY. He FLOSSES every night, so his teeth beat everybody else's. Ask: for three or more, comparative or superlative? 'Cleaner' compares only two.
hints.S37_B5: BLEEDING cannot be counted - you never say 'one bleeding, two bleedings'. Ask: which choice partners an uncountable noun? 'Few', 'many' and 'several' all need things you can count one by one.
hints.S37_B6: NOT sits in front of the gap, and two clinics are being compared for EXPENSIVE treatment. Ask: which pair keeps both prices level, so that 'not' can then tip one lower? 'More … than' would already declare one dearer.
hints.S37_B7: The BROKEN TOOTH could not fix itself - BY THE DENTIST names who acted, and the APPOINTMENT is over. Ask: which choice is passive and past? Passive = a form of 'be' + past participle.
hints.S37_B8: TOLD THE PATIENT = reported speech, and it is an instruction about SUGARY DRINKS. Ask: after 'told' + person, which verb form follows - plain, -ing, past, or an infinitive? Only one of them can carry an order.
hints.S37_C1: Two facts clash: Liam is NERVOUS inside, yet he walks in CALMLY. Ask: which joining word signals a contrast? 'Because' would claim the nerves caused the calm, which makes no sense.
hints.S37_C2: His HEART BEAT FASTER at the exact instant the drill was SWITCHED ON - one sudden point in time. Ask: which conjunction marks a single moment rather than a long stretch? A stretch word needs an ongoing action.
hints.S37_C3: Two long actions overlap: Liam COUNTED THE CEILING TILES and the dentist WAS WORKING on his tooth. Ask: which conjunction joins two actions running side by side? A point-in-time word suits a sudden event, not a slow one.
hints.S37_C4: The second half explains WHY he felt no PAIN: the ANAESTHETIC HAD NUMBED his gum. Ask: which conjunction gives a plain, direct reason? A contrast word would deny the link instead of stating it.
hints.S37_C5: HAS TREATED reaches from the past right up to today, and SIX YEARS OLD is the starting point. Ask: which conjunction means 'from that time until now'? A pure reason word cannot mark a starting point.
hints.S37_C6: Raising his hand depends on something that may never happen: DISCOMFORT during the procedure. Ask: which conjunction sets a condition? A time word would promise that the discomfort is certain to come.
hints.S37_C7: The DECAY WOULD SPREAD in one case only: the FILLING was NOT done that day. Ask: which single conjunction already carries a hidden negative inside it, so you never have to add one?
hints.S37_C8: THE MINUTES PASSED and, little by little, the TIGHTNESS in his shoulders EASED - both changes creep along together. Ask: which conjunction fits gradual, side-by-side change? A sudden-moment word would jar here.
hints.S37_D1: The clue is right in the sentence: HARD OUTER LAYER THAT PROTECTS THE TOOTH, worn away by SUGAR. Ask: which box word names that protective coat? The sticky film forms on top of it - it is not the tooth's own layer.
hints.S37_D2: BACTERIA combine with FOOD PARTICLES to form a STICKY COATING on the surface of the teeth. Ask: which box word names that film? A hole in the tooth comes later, and it is not the coating itself.
hints.S37_D3: The sentence defines it for you: A SMALL HOLE THAT DEVELOPS IN THE TOOTH after TOOTH DECAY. Ask: which box word names that hole? The sticky film and the hard outer layer are not holes.
hints.S37_D4: You already BRUSH TWICE A DAY; this second action cleans BETWEEN OUR TEETH, where the TOOTHBRUSH CANNOT REACH. Ask: which box word is the verb for using thin thread between the teeth?
hints.S37_D5: Dentists INJECT MEDICINE so the patient DOES NOT FEEL ANY PAIN during the procedure. Ask: which box word is the verb meaning to take all feeling away from an area? A noun cannot follow 'medicine to ___'.
hints.S37_E1: Stretch the underlined word into its long form and read it before IMPORTANT: does 'belonging to it' make any sense? Ask: which spelling can be opened out into two words? A possessive never can. Test by expanding, not by sound.
hints.S37_E2: BRUSHED is an action, and the underlined word tells you HOW the brushing was done. Ask: does an action need an adjective, or a word carrying the -ly ending? Adjectives describe nouns, never verbs.
hints.S37_E3: TOOTHS is the trap: this noun does not build its plural with -s at all. Ask: how do you write more than one FOOT, or more than one goose? The same kind of change happens here - the vowels shift.
hints.S37_E4: Count the subject: THE CHILDREN, not one child. Ask: does a plural subject take 'was', or its plural partner? Match the verb to the subject, never to the word standing nearest to it.
hints.S37_E5: PAINFULLER crams an ending onto a two-syllable adjective. Ask: do long adjectives take -er, or do they need a helper word placed in front? Compare: careful, helpful, useful - none of them take -er.
hints.S37_F1: One sentence is a cause, one is a result. She has NEVER HAD A CAVITY - is that the reason, or the outcome? Ask: after 'Since', which half must come first? Then a comma separates the two halves.
hints.S37_F2: 'Unless' packs a hidden negative inside itself, so nothing else in that half may be negative. Ask: which half is the condition - FLOSS EVERY DAY, or the state of your TEETH? And can 'will' ever sit after 'unless'?
